case_study_insert.main_stem: Tropicfruit Exports (TFE) is a partnership in the fresh-fruit export sector, based near Accra and employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Kwame Boateng, it exports graded mangoes to European importers and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. TFE plans to invest $560,000 in a new packhouse and refrigerated cold chain, financed by a $360,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $11 a unit and a selling price of $23, and produces 60,000 units a year. TFE faces post-harvest spoilage of 8% of the crop and labour turnover of 12% among its packhouse staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Packhouse Quality Log — Q1 2025: The packhouse handled 15,400 cartons last quarter at a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.2% a year earlier. Rejected consignments fell from 27 to 15 a month. Average time from picking to dispatch was 2.6 days. A survey of 480 importers found 62% would pay $0.40 more for premium graded mangoes, and 49% check phytosanitary certification. Post-harvest loss was 8% of the crop. A skills audit shows 10 of 48 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new graders; off-the-job training at the agricultural institute costs $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tropicfruit Exports as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Export Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing the cost of the $360,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.30 to $14.22 an hour, raising packhouse payroll costs. (3) Packaging and refrigerated-freight input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, while export demand for tropical fruit grew 4.7%.

questions.question_text: TFE is funding its $560,000 packhouse and refrigerated cold chain with a $360,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TFE of using retained profit instead of borrowing the full amount.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so TFE protects cash flow against fixed costs of $180,000 a year while it repays the $360,000 loan. Every dollar of the $200,000 not borrowed can absorb the 10.2% rise in packaging and refrigerated-freight costs, helping Kwame Boateng hold the $23 selling price for European importers.

Point 2: Using $200,000 retained profit reduces the amount secured against the partnership's assets, so the new packhouse is less exposed to bank action if export demand slips below the 15,400 cartons handled last quarter. It also keeps decision-making with the partners, letting them respond to the 62% of 480 importers willing to pay $0.40 more for premium graded mangoes without lender conditions attached to extra borrowing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TFE's financing decision.

questions.question_text: TFE is promoting its premium graded mangoes to European importers. Consider a regional television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TFE choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television: TV would give TFE wide reach and show the mangoes being graded, but airtime is expensive for a partnership with $180,000 fixed costs and a $360,000 loan, and most viewers are not European importers. Much of the budget would be wasted on consumers who cannot buy export cartons, so television is poorly matched to the $560,000 packhouse investment.

Local newspaper advertising: Newspapers are cheaper and can reach local suppliers and packhouse workers, and ads can support sourcing. Their limit is that the audience is not the European buyer deciding on the 49% who check phytosanitary certification, and print cannot show fruit quality, so orders beyond the 15,400-carton baseline are unlikely to grow.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and travel influencers can show graded mangoes and the phytosanitary story to international audiences, with engagement measured against the 2.6-day dispatch time and 15,400 cartons. Results build slowly and depend on credible partners, but cost per reached buyer is low and the content can support the 62% of 480 importers willing to pay $0.40 more.

Recommendation: TFE should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by direct contact with known importers. It reaches overseas buyers that local newspapers cannot and shows product quality far more cheaply than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $560,000 investment; local newspapers are rejected because their readership is not the export customer TFE needs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TFE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TFE with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: TFE's labour turnover has reached 12% under laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for TFE of introducing job enrichment in its workforce of 48.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives the 48 packhouse staff more responsibility for grading and dispatch decisions, increasing satisfaction and commitment under laissez-faire leadership. Higher morale should reduce the 12% labour turnover that forces repeated hiring, protecting the 15,400-carton quarterly output and the 2.6-day picking-to-dispatch time for European importers.

Point 2: Staff who own their grading work are more likely to spot defects early, cutting the 2.9% defect rate and the 8% post-harvest loss. That protects the $23 selling price and $12 contribution, helps answer the 62% of 480 importers willing to pay $0.40 more, and reduces the need to retrain the 10 of 48 staff missing on-the-job training at $700 each while the $560,000 cold chain beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TFE's turnover, spoilage and export operation.

questions.question_text: TFE must train 10 of 48 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new graders. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the agricultural institute. Which should TFE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the graders is tailored to TFE's own quality standards and keeps the 10 trainees productive during the 15,400-carton quarter. It can directly reduce the 2.9% defect rate and 8% post-harvest loss because supervisors correct grading immediately. Drawbacks are that busy packers have limited time to teach, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate to reassure the 49% of importers checking phytosanitary certification.

Off-the-job training: The agricultural institute course at $700 per employee costs 10 × $700 = $7,000, small beside the $560,000 investment. It gives structured grading and food-safety skills plus a recognised certificate useful for European importers. However, it removes 10 of 48 staff from the packhouse during peak season, risking dispatch slower than the current 2.6 days, and generic content will still need adaptation to TFE's graders.

Decision: TFE should choose on-the-job training for immediate rollout, adding short certified institute modules later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids slowing the 2.6-day dispatch while 12% labour turnover already disrupts the workforce of 48. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost shifts and $7,000 fee would hit the 15,400-carton operation and the generic course would not cover TFE's exact graders. A pilot on one grading line should compare the 2.9% defect rate and 8% loss before TFE commits $7,000 to all 10 staff.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TFE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of TFE.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TFE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate TFE's average total cost per carton.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = Fixed cost per unit + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ 60,000 units = $3.00, plus $11.00 = $14.00. Answer: average total cost is $14.00 a carton.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $23.00 − $11.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TFE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Average total cost of $14.00 against the $23.00 price gives a $9.00 margin a carton, a benchmark for the new cold chain and for cutting the 8% post-harvest loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets managers test a discount for importers: cutting the $23.00 price by $1 to $22.00 leaves $11.00 contribution, so they can judge whether extra orders offset the loss before using the $0.40 premium mentioned by 62% of 480 importers.
3. With fixed costs of $180,000 and $12.00 contribution, break-even is $180,000 ÷ $12.00 = 15,000 cartons; against 60,000 cartons that leaves a margin of safety of 45,000, showing how much export demand can fall before losses.
4. Managers can compare unit cost with the $700 training fee and 10 untrained staff to decide whether reducing the 2.9% defect rate pays, and review the $11.00 variable cost given 10.2% freight and packaging inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Average total cost = $14.00 | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: $14.00 cost versus $23.00 price and 8% loss; $12.00 contribution for discount decisions; 15,000-carton break-even and 45,000 safety margin; and $700 training spend benchmark against 10 untrained staff.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TFE's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TFE's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.64 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.74 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.22 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $75,000 inventories + $65,000 trade receivables + $32,000 cash = $172,000; 2025 current assets = $58,000 + $82,000 + $55,000 = $195,000. For 2024, $172,000 ÷ $105,000 = 1.64 and ($172,000 − $75,000) ÷ $105,000 = $97,000 ÷ $105,000 = 0.92. For 2025, $195,000 ÷ $112,000 = 1.74 and ($195,000 − $58,000) ÷ $112,000 = $137,000 ÷ $112,000 = 1.22.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The first ratio rose from 1.64 to 1.74 because current assets grew from $172,000 to $195,000 faster than current liabilities, which increased from $105,000 to $112,000. The second measure climbed from 0.92 to 1.22, so TFE can now meet short-term obligations without relying on selling $58,000 of perishable mango stock, valuable while a $360,000 loan and a $560,000 packhouse are outstanding. The caution is trade receivables, up from $65,000 to $82,000, which lock away cash if European importers pay late, and 12% labour turnover could disrupt the 2.6-day dispatch promise.

Conclusion: TFE's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not depend on inventory, so short-term solvency is stronger. Rising receivables are the main risk, so the partners should tighten credit control as the cold chain starts up.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: TFE is considering a certified premium grade for its mangoes. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TFE of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A certified premium grade matches the 62% of 480 importers who would pay $0.40 more and the 49% who check phytosanitary certification, protecting the $12.00 contribution per carton against 10.2% packaging and freight inflation. It also supports the $560,000 packhouse and cold-chain investment by differentiating TFE's mangoes from ungraded fruit.

Disadvantage: Certification and inspection costs are not quantified in the insert, so the net benefit cannot be calculated. Stricter grading could raise the 2.9% defect rate or the 8% post-harvest loss if more fruit is rejected, and consignments missed against the 2.6-day dispatch time could damage the 15,400-carton relationship with European importers. TFE should trial the grade with one importer before extending it to all exports.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TFE's survey, costs and quality data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in packaging and refrigerated-freight input costs will affect TFE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If TFE's $360,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $360,000 = $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates may also make the 4.7% growth in export demand harder to finance and raise the cost of any future borrowing for the $560,000 project.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.22 an hour): TFE's workforce of 48 includes hourly-paid packhouse staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 48 staff = 1,250 cartons per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds; cutting 12% labour turnover and training the 10 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (10.2%): Packaging and refrigerated freight feed the $11.00 variable cost on every carton. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $11.00 were exposed, 10.2% × $11.00 = $1.122, about $1.12 a carton, and at 60,000 units that is roughly $67,320 a year (60,000 × $1.122). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $12.00 contribution on every carton and recurs with each export order.

Conclusion: The 10.2% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats across 60,000 cartons and directly attacks the $12.00 contribution that services the $360,000 loan and the $560,000 packhouse, whereas the interest rise costs $2,700 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 1,250 cartons per worker. TFE should cut the 8% post-harvest loss and seek the $0.40 premium from 62% of importers rather than absorb the whole rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TFE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TFE's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
